Skip to main contentFor devs working on model training for AI Infrastructure or AI Platforms, does GPU compute efficiency matter? For devs working on model training for AI Infrastructure or AI Platforms, does GPU compute efficiency matter? * At companies that focuses on a few but large models, it would matter because it would create cost savings (GPUs are expensive). If one's AI/ML Platform team would require more features for users, then that would be prioritized over spending time making models run faster. I also observed that each model itself would have different ways of being optimized to train or run faster. In my case I once optimized the training time if a model down to 6 hours from 24 hours, the user was really excited but they still asked can we maybe get it down to 4 or 2 when using stuff like Fp16 or xla or what else. Yeah it makes sense most AI and ML solutions companies really just use a pretrained model but I did not expect such models are even infra optimized too. This combined with the massive costs of training a LLM from scratch and the number of people focusing on these model types. Imo if you are actually working with AI, such that teams are working specifically on training models specifically for your business the cost should not be a factor because the benefits outweighs any cost your business would incur. Yes, as inefficient GPU utilisation prolongs training (as model might be waiting for data, so the overall util will be low) and queueing times (GPUs are finite, if an inefficient model is hogging X GPUs, it will take longer for them to be freed). So scheduling efficiency is huge, but what about individual gpu utilization or model training optimization? Training efficiency matters a lot if training or fine tuning large models (eg; LLMs) since the total cost can be in the millions or tens of millions of dollars. results.content: # The role of GPU memory for training large language models. While GPU compute capabilities have dramatically increased thanks to advances like GPU cores handling reduced precision formats, memory systems haven’t kept pace. This growing imbalance between compute and memory, known as the memory wall, has become a key bottleneck in training ever-larger deep learning models. We must examine the fundamental computations within neural networks to understand why memory bandwidth impedes model scaling. Reducing data movement and increasing data reuse in model architectures and training algorithms is imperative to combat the memory wall. Absent these innovations, memory bandwidth continues to throttle the realization of ever larger and more powerful AI models. To continue reaping accuracy gains from larger models, innovations in memory architectures, data encoding, and movement-reducing algorithms have become critical priorities. From 2016 to 2022, GPU memory capacity expanded five times, while compute increased 46 times.

What are the memory requirements for training a transformer model? Training a transformer model requires significant memory resources, primarily due to the model's architecture, batch size, sequence length, and precision settings. The memory requirements can vary widely depending on the specific model size, optimization techniques, and hardware configuration. Below, we break down the key factors influencing memory consumption during transformer model training. ### Key Factors Affecting Memory Requirements * **Model Size:** The number of parameters in the model directly impacts memory usage. For example, GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters requires substantially more memory than smaller models like BERT-base (110 million parameters). Reducing batch size can lower memory usage but may affect training stability. * **Precision:** Training in full precision (FP32) consumes more memory than mixed-precision training (FP16 or BF16). * **Optimization Techniques:** Methods like gradient checkpointing, model parallelism, and activation offloading can reduce memory usage at the cost of computational overhead. ### Memory Estimates for Common Transformer Models ### GPU Recommendations for Training Transformers To efficiently train transformer models, high-memory GPUs with fast interconnects are essential. Here are some recommended NVIDIA GPUs for different scales of transformer training: * **Small to Medium Models (e.g., BERT, GPT-2):** NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48GB), A40 (48GB), or L40S (48GB) provide sufficient memory for most mid-sized models. * **Large Models (e.g., GPT-3, T5):** NVIDIA A100 (80GB PCIe/SXM4) or H100 (80GB PCIe/SXM5) are ideal due to their high memory capacity and Tensor Core acceleration. * **Extremely Large Models (e.g., GPT-4 class):** Multi-GPU setups with NVIDIA H100 NVL (188GB per GPU) or A100 clusters with NVLink are necessary for distributed training. ### Optimizing Memory Usage To reduce memory requirements without sacrificing model performance, consider the following techniques: 1. 2. **Mixed Precision Training:** Using FP16 or BF16 with NVIDIA Tensor Cores can halve memory consumption while maintaining model accuracy. 3. **Model Parallelism:** Splitting the model across multiple GPUs or nodes can enable training of models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. Understanding these factors and leveraging the right hardware can help optimize memory usage and accelerate transformer model training.

results.title: LLM GPU Memory Calculator — Twinko AI
results.content: ### LLM GPU Memory Consumption Calculator. ### References & Credits. The GPU memory calculation strategies and insights into the challenges of training large language models (LLMs) are inspired by the lessons from Generative AI with Large Language Models course by deeplearning.ai. Specifically, the sections on "Optional video: Efficient multi-GPU compute strategies" and "Computational challenges of training LLMs" provided valuable information for developing this calculator. ### Calculation Method, Logic, and Training Overhead Explained. The calculator estimates GPU memory required using the formula:. * **Total Training Memory:** Storage Memory \* (1 + Training Overhead Multiplier). Where the training overhead multiplier accounts for:. * Two optimizer states (16 or 8 bytes, matching precision). * Activations and temporary variables (estimated at 5 times the model storage memory). The training overhead multiplier is approximately 6, assuming 1 for model storage and 5 for the additional components, calculated per parameter in bytes:. Reduced memory with minimal precision loss. Maximum memory efficiency with more significant precision loss. Final formula for memory calculation: *Memory (GB) = Parameters (billions) \* BytesPerParameter \* 6 / (1024^3)*. ### Understanding Multi-GPU Compute Strategies. **Distributed Data Parallel (DDP):** This strategy replicates your model on each GPU, processing data in parallel and synchronizing the results to update the model identically across all GPUs. It's efficient for models that fit within a single GPU's memory, speeding up training by leveraging parallel computation. **Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP):** FSDP extends capabilities for larger models by sharding model states across GPUs, reducing memory redundancy. Inspired by the ZeRO optimization, it distributes model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, enabling training of models too large for a single GPU. Choosing between DDP and FSDP depends on your model's size and the memory capacity of your GPUs. FSDP allows for scaling to larger models by minimizing memory footprint, while DDP is simpler and efficient for models that easily fit in memory.

As you are already aware that the GPU can be leveraged for model training in PhysicsAI, however, there are a few important points which should be considered to make sure that the GPU gets utilized by PhysicsAI for the same. 1. Checking GPU compatibility with PhysicsAI: Make sure that the GPU being considered has the correct specifications in terms of the ‘Compute Capability’. 3. However, there have been instances of GPU usage (CUDA graphs) not being shown in the Windows Task Manager & hence, the above-mentioned suggestions can serve useful to check if GPU/CPU is being used for the PhysicsAI model training. 2. Once GPU has the Compute Capability of greater than 6.0, CUDA Toolkit 11.8 & CUDNN 8.7 version are installed, then PhysicsAI would automatically use the GPU for the model training & the log file under ‘PhysicsAI>Model training>Show Log’  will have the GPU memory usage displayed (as shown in Figure 3) at the end of the training log. Figure 3 : GPU usage by PhysicsAI for the model training indicated by the ‘Model Training Log’. * **Disabling GPU usage for PhysicsAI model training**. Once GPU is detected by PhysicsAI, it will automatically be used for the model training. This would serve useful in scenarios where the GPU does not have enough memory to train the model due to various reasons related to the number of elements/nodes in the model, model hyper-parameters such as width/depth/epochs & gives the PhysicsAI error as *‘Resources exhausted during training - Try reducing width, depth or size of the mesh’*. * **Memory consumption by GPU for the PhysicsAI model training:**. For example: if a batch size of 1 is used, only one model (mesh) resides on the GPU at a time & hence, the peak memory usage is governed by the largest model (mesh) in the training data & not on the number of training meshes in total used for the model training.
